questions.question: You run ghci> :load Hello.hs and see 'Ok, one module loaded.' Has 'Hello, World!' been printed yet?
options: No — :load only checks and loads the definitions; main has to be typed and run separately
Yes, but only the first time the file is loaded
No, and it never will be printed because :load does not support IO actions
questions.explanation: Loading compiles and type-checks the file and makes its top-level definitions available at the prompt. It does not run anything. main only performs its action once you type main and press Enter.
optionFeedback: :load's job stops at making the module's definitions available; it does not decide to run any of them, including main.

Correct. The lesson's four-step trace is explicit: 'You saved a definition... GHCi compiled and loaded it... You named the action... The effect became visible' — loading and running are two separate steps.
Whether it is the first load or a reload, :load never runs main by itself; you always have to name it.
main is loaded successfully and can absolutely be run afterwards — nothing about :load disables IO.

check-three-ways-to-run-a-script.title: Check: three ways to run a script

questions.question: You want to hand a finished lab in as a program someone else can double-click or run without installing GHC's interactive tools every time. Which approach fits best?
options: ghc -o hello Hello.hs, then run the resulting executable
Typing the whole program directly at the ghci> prompt
questions.explanation: Compiling with ghc -o produces a standalone executable — the only one of the three approaches that leaves behind a program runnable on its own, independent of GHCi or runhaskell being invoked again.
optionFeedback: :load requires an interactive GHCi session every time; it leaves no standalone artefact for someone else to run.
runhaskell also recompiles and runs the script fresh each time; like :load, it leaves nothing behind that can be run independently.
Correct. This is the row in the table marked 'Yes' under 'Leaves an executable?' — exactly the property this scenario needs.
Individual expressions can be typed at the prompt, but a whole saved program is not meant to be retyped by hand, and nothing would be left behind afterwards either.

questions.question: Wrong.hs contains module Test where and loads successfully on its own with :load Wrong.hs. A second file containing import Test is then loaded. What happens, and why?
options: It loads fine, because Haskell locates modules by their declared name, not their filename
It fails with 'Could not find module Test', because GHC locates an imported module by looking for a file with that same name — Test.hs, not Wrong.hs
It fails only because Wrong.hs is an unusual filename to choose
Both files load, but calling any function from Test silently does nothing
questions.explanation: The callout gives this exact case: loading a mismatched file directly still works, but 'the rule bites as soon as another module imports it, because GHC locates a module by looking for a file of the same name.' Test is never found, because the file is not called Test.hs.
optionFeedback: It is exactly the reverse: GHC's module search for an import looks for a matching filename, which is why the mismatch only causes a problem once an import is involved.
Correct — this is the precise failure shown in the callout's transcript: Could not find module 'Test', because import searches by filename.
Any filename would trigger the identical failure once its internal module name disagrees with it; 'Wrong.hs' is simply the name chosen for this example, not the cause.
The import fails to resolve at all, so nothing from Test becomes available to call — this is a load-time error, not a silent no-op at call time.
